s: Forbes profile, real-time net worth $4.2B as of 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time billionaire figure; Forbes notes he holds over 2% of Datadog
did: Co-founded Datadog in New York in 2010 with Alexis Le-Quoc, selling cloud infrastructure monitoring as a per-host SaaS subscription; took it public on Nasdaq in September 2019 at $27 a share, where it doubled on day one.
why: Existing tools were built either for sysadmins or for developers, and the two sides could not see the same graph. Datadog sold one dashboard to both, self-serve on a credit card, so it spread inside a company the way AWS did - bottom up, per host, with no procurement cycle.
obst: They raised only about $15M in the first five years because investors thought infrastructure monitoring was a commodity already owned by Nagios and New Relic, and the pair had to build the product while consulting to pay salaries.
turn: Turning down a roughly $1B acquisition approach from Cisco in 2016 and staying independent to the IPO.

s: Forbes profile, real-time net worth $4.0B as of 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time billionaire figure
did: Founded Paulson and Co in 1994 as a small merger-arbitrage fund, then in 2006 and 2007 bought credit default swaps on subprime mortgage bonds and the BBB tranches of the ABX index, making about $15B for his funds and roughly $4B personally in 2007.
why: The asymmetry was mechanical, not clairvoyant: protection on a BBB subprime tranche cost about 1% a year while paying near par on default, so he could be wrong for three years and still win once. Rating agencies were stamping AAA on pools of 2006-vintage no-doc loans.
obst: The trade bled premium through 2006 and investors redeemed; later his gold fund fell about 35% in 2013, the Sino-Forest position was wiped out by a short-seller report, and assets collapsed from roughly $38B to under $10B before he converted to a family office in 2020.
turn: The collapse of the ABX index in early 2007, which turned a carry cost into the largest single-year trading gain on record.

s: Forbes profile, real-time net worth $3.2B as of 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time billionaire figure, built from JPMorgan restricted stock disclosed in Form 4 filings
did: Left American Express with Sandy Weill in 1986 to take over Commercial Credit, rolled it up into Primerica, Travelers and then Citigroup; fired in 1998, he took over Bank One in 2000, sold it to JPMorgan in 2004 and has run JPMorgan since 2006.
why: He refused to hold the structured mortgage inventory his peers carried into 2007, so JPMorgan entered the crisis with capital while rivals needed it. That let the bank buy Bear Stearns at $10 a share and Washington Mutual's deposits for $1.9B - franchises bought at the bottom, paid off for fifteen years.
obst: Weill fired him in November 1998 and he spent sixteen months unemployed; then the 2012 London Whale derivatives loss of $6.2B, a $920M penalty and a Senate investigation, followed by throat cancer in 2014.
turn: The March 2008 weekend purchase of Bear Stearns, which established JPMorgan as the buyer of last resort.

s: Forbes profile, net worth $2.9B (Richard LeFrak and family)
m: Published Forbes figure for the LeFrak family holding
did: Third-generation head of the LeFrak Organization, which owns rather than trades: 5,000 apartments across twenty buildings at LeFrak City in Queens, the 600-acre Newport district built on Jersey City rail yards, and now SoLe Mia in North Miami.
why: LeFrak builds at cost, holds forever and never syndicates. Middle-income towers put up in the 1960s at construction cost still collect rent sixty years later against a depreciated basis, and the Jersey City waterfront was bought as contaminated rail land nobody else would underwrite.
obst: LeFrak City deteriorated through the 1970s and the family settled a federal housing-discrimination suit in 1972; New York's 2019 rent law then capped increases on the stabilized apartments that are the core of the portfolio.
turn: The 1986 purchase of the derelict Jersey City waterfront that became Newport.

s: Forbes profile, real-time net worth $2.7B as of 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time billionaire figure
did: Buys Manhattan storefronts - Fifth Avenue, Times Square, SoHo, Madison - and re-leases them to global flagship tenants; his Wharton Properties assembled and partly sold 717 Fifth Avenue and controls much of the Fifth Avenue luxury corridor.
why: He underwrites the lease, not the building. Buying a tired storefront and signing a European luxury house that needs a New York flagship for prestige rather than profit converts a retail space into a bond, and the cap rate on the new rent revalues the whole asset overnight.
obst: Fifth Avenue asking rents fell by more than half between 2016 and 2020 and vacancies opened along his corridor; he handed back several heavily levered properties and fought a public and litigious split with a long-time partner.
turn: The 2011 purchase of 720 Fifth Avenue with SL Green and its re-leasing at record rents, which proved the flagship-rent arbitrage at scale.

s: Forbes profile, real-time net worth $2.3B as of 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time billionaire figure; Mars bought a majority of KIND in 2020 at a reported $5B valuation
did: Founded KIND in 2004 selling fruit-and-nut bars in transparent wrappers with whole ingredients visible through the plastic; sold a minority to VMG Partners in 2014 and a majority to Mars in November 2020 at a reported $5B valuation.
why: The clear wrapper was the claim. Every competitor had to argue on the label that its extruded bar was healthy; KIND simply let you see five whole almonds, which removed the trust problem, and he pushed the bars through Starbucks, airports and hospital gift shops where snack buyers had no alternatives.
obst: In March 2015 the FDA sent a warning letter ordering KIND to remove the word healthy from four labels because the nuts pushed saturated fat over the threshold - a rule written for 1990s low-fat science.
turn: Petitioning the FDA rather than complying quietly; the agency reversed in 2016 and later rewrote the healthy definition, and the fight became national free publicity.

s: Forbes profile, real-time net worth $2.2B as of 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time billionaire figure
did: With his sister Sonia Gardner founded Amroc Investments in 1989 to trade bankruptcy claims, then Avenue Capital in 1995, now about $13B in distressed debt; bought the Milwaukee Bucks for $550M in 2014 with Wes Edens and sold at a $3.5B valuation in 2023.
why: Distressed paper is sold by mandate, not by judgment - insurers and mutual funds must dump a bond the day it is downgraded. Buying at thirty cents from a forced seller and then leading the creditors committee lets him write the reorganization plan and convert the debt into the equity of the surviving company.
obst: Avenue's flagship fund fell about 25% in 2008 and investors gated; assets fell from roughly $19B to $12B, and the Asian funds shrank as the distressed cycle failed to arrive there.
turn: Buying Donald Trump's Taj Mahal casino bonds at a deep discount around 1990 and being repaid, which made the siblings names in distressed credit.

s: Forbes profile, real-time net worth $2.2B as of 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time billionaire figure
did: Left Leon Cooperman's Omega Advisors to found Glenview Capital in Manhattan in 2000 with about $100M; ran a concentrated long-biased equity fund that peaked near $10B, and made his defining bet in 2012-13 on hospital operators HCA, Tenet and Health Management ahead of the Affordable Care Act.
why: He read the ACA as a volume event rather than a policy debate: hospitals were already treating uninsured patients in emergency rooms and booking the cost as bad debt, so coverage expansion converted existing patients into paying ones with no new capacity. He sized it far past normal diversification limits.
obst: Glenview lost roughly 18% in 2015 and fell again in 2016, and assets halved as investors left; his Health Management Associates campaign required replacing the entire board by written consent, which the company litigated.
turn: The August 2013 written-consent sweep of the Health Management Associates board, which forced the sale to Community Health.

s: Forbes profile, real-time net worth $2.1B as of 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes figure based on her Loews Corporation stake and the family New York Giants interest Started dated to her father Preston Robert Tisch death in Nov 2005, when the stake passed to her; an heir crosses $100M on inheritance, so time-to-first-$100M is zero.
did: Daughter of Preston Robert Tisch, she holds a share of the Loews Corporation fortune and of the family half of the New York Giants, bought for $75M in 1991; she runs the Illumination Fund, which financed New York's Green Carts produce vendors and arts access programs.
why: Loews buys entire businesses in unloved industries at book value and holds them - cigarettes through Lorillard, offshore drilling through Diamond, insurance through CNA. The Giants stake compounded on a different engine: the NFL national television contract, split equally across 32 clubs.
obst: She and her brother pushed against cousins running Loews over strategy and were bought out of parts of the family position; the Lorillard tobacco holding carried decades of product liability litigation culminating in the 1998 Master Settlement Agreement.
turn: The 1991 purchase of 50% of the New York Giants for $75M, an asset now valued in the billions.

s: Forbes profile, real-time net worth $1.7B as of 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time billionaire figure, based on his Blue Owl Capital stake
did: After 22 years at KKR building its energy and infrastructure business, co-founded Owl Rock Capital in 2016 with Doug Ostrover and Craig Packer to lend directly to mid-market private-equity-owned companies; merged with Dyal Capital in a 2021 SPAC to form Blue Owl, now about $250B of assets.
why: Post-crisis capital rules pushed leveraged lending out of banks, and the borrowers were sponsors who value certainty of close over price. Owl Rock raised the money in permanent-capital BDC vehicles, so management fees are charged on capital that never has to be returned - an annuity, not a fund.
obst: No institution wants to anchor a first-time direct-lending manager with a billion dollars, and they had to build scale before a credit cycle tested them; the 2021 Dyal transaction drew litigation from Sixth Street and Golub over the sale of stakes in their own firms.
turn: The 2021 SPAC merger with Dyal, which converted private fee streams into permanently listed public equity.

s: Forbes profile, $1.1B as of 3 Jun 2026 (Americas Richest Self-Made Women)
m: Published Forbes figure; corroborated by her disclosed 17.8M Alclear Holdings units in 2026 Form 4 filings
did: A hedge fund manager at Arience Capital who in 2010 bought the assets of the bankrupt airport-security startup Verified Identity Pass for about $6M with Ken Cornick, rebuilt it as CLEAR, and took it public on the NYSE in June 2021 at roughly a $4.5B valuation.
why: She bought the two things that take a decade to build - TSA certification and an enrolled member database - for the price of a Manhattan apartment. Everything after that was distribution: airlines and stadiums gave up lane space because CLEAR members arrive early and spend, so the network expanded without capital.
obst: The predecessor company had collapsed in 2009 after losing a laptop holding 33,000 applicants data; airports had cancelled the contracts and abandoned members were furious, so she had to re-sign every airport and rebuild federal trust from a bankruptcy estate.
turn: The 2010 bankruptcy asset purchase for roughly $6M, which bought a federally certified identity network for scrap value.

s: Permira take-private of Squarespace closed Oct 2024 at $7.2B enterprise value; merger proxy discloses Casalena rolling at least 75% of his existing equity
m: Pre-deal founder stake of roughly 12% of equity x $7.2B transaction value = about $0.86B, substantially rolled rather than cashed
did: Wrote Squarespace alone in a University of Maryland dorm room in 2003 and ran it with no employees and no outside money for seven years; raised $38.5M from Accel and Index in 2010, direct-listed on the NYSE in 2021, and sold to Permira in 2024 at $7.2B while rolling most of his stake.
why: He owned the entire stack - hosting, templates, domains, email, commerce - so a restaurant or photographer got a professional site with no developer and one bill. Then he bought distribution wholesale through podcast sponsorship, before anyone else had priced that channel.
obst: Seven years bootstrapped and alone against venture-funded rivals; then the 2012 Squarespace 6 rebuild risked breaking every existing customer site at once, and the 2021 direct listing opened below the reference price into a collapsing software market.
turn: The 2010 first venture round paired with the podcast advertising campaign that turned a hosting product into a consumer brand.

s: WallStreetZen insider ownership table: 1,954,007 MongoDB shares; MDB closed $430.83 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 1,954,007 shares x $430.83 = $841.8M; excludes DoubleClick proceeds and other holdings
did: Co-founded DoubleClick in 1996 and wrote its ad-serving engine, then in 2007 co-founded 10gen with Kevin Ryan and Eliot Horowitz; 10gen built and open-sourced MongoDB, became MongoDB Inc and listed on Nasdaq in 2017. He remains a director and one of its largest individual holders.
why: DoubleClick's own database failures taught him that relational schemas break under web-scale write volume. Open-sourcing MongoDB put it on every developer laptop before any CIO heard the name, so adoption preceded the sales call instead of following it - the enterprise contract was a formality after the fact.
obst: MongoDB was mocked for years over unacknowledged writes and data-loss defaults, which forced the 2014 WiredTiger acquisition and a storage-engine rewrite; then Amazon cloned the API as DocumentDB in 2019, forcing the SSPL licence change and a fight with the open-source community.
turn: The 2009 decision to open-source the database under AGPL rather than sell it as a licensed product.

s: Forbes, Jul 2025, reported Meyer holds about 3.5M Shake Shack shares; SHAK closed $75.82 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 3.5M shares x $75.82 = $265M, plus Union Square Hospitality Group equity and roughly $400M of disclosed prior SHAK share sales since the 2015 IPO
co: Union Square Hospitality Group and Shake Shack
did: Opened Union Square Cafe in 1985 at 27, built Gramercy Tavern, Eleven Madison Park and Blue Smoke, then turned a 2001 hot dog cart in Madison Square Park into Shake Shack and took it public in January 2015 at $21 a share.
why: Shake Shack began as a fundraiser for the Madison Square Park Conservancy, so it launched with a queue and a civic story instead of an advertising budget. He then ran fine-dining hiring and service standards inside a fast-food cost structure, which let him charge $9 for a burger in a $5 category.
obst: He abolished tipping across all Union Square Hospitality restaurants in 2015 and had to reverse it in 2020 after staff turnover and guest resistance; covid then closed every restaurant and he laid off about 2,000 staff in March 2020.
turn: The January 2015 Shake Shack IPO, which doubled on the first day and revalued a hot dog cart as a public company.

s: Forbes profile, last published figure $1.0B as of Mar 2014
m: Forbes last valued him at $1B in 2014; discounted here for his subsequent disclosed Capri Holdings share sales and the stock decline since 2014
did: Launched his womenswear label in 1981 selling to Bergdorf Goodman, went bankrupt in 1993, relaunched with Sportswear Holdings backing, designed Celine for LVMH from 1997, launched the accessible-luxury Michael Michael Kors line in 2004 and listed the company in December 2011.
why: The diffusion line hit an empty price point: a $300 handbag sat between $80 Coach and $1,500 European luxury exactly as American outlet-mall traffic peaked. Judging Project Runway from 2004 then supplied national brand awareness that no fashion house could have bought at that stage.
obst: His company filed for bankruptcy in 1993 and the label went dark for two years; a decade after the IPO the same outlet channel that built the brand made it ubiquitous, full-price margins collapsed and Capri's shares fell more than 60% from their 2014 peak.
turn: The 2004 launch of Michael Michael Kors, which moved the brand from runway to mall.

s: WallStreetZen insider ownership table: 1,568,212 MongoDB shares; MDB closed $430.83 on 21 Aug 2026
did: Co-founded 10gen in 2007 with Dwight Merriman and Kevin Ryan after building ad-serving systems at DoubleClick and ShopWiki; wrote much of the original MongoDB server and was chief technology officer until 2020. He now runs Viam, a New York robotics software company.
why: Developers, not chief information officers, picked the database. MongoDB stored documents that matched the JSON objects application code already used, which deleted the object-relational mapping layer that every Rails and Node team hated. Removing a chore beat winning a benchmark.
obst: Early MongoDB defaulted to fire-and-forget writes and the company spent years answering public accusations of silent data loss, which forced the WiredTiger acquisition in 2014 and a full storage-engine replacement before enterprises would sign.
turn: The 2009 open-source release, which turned the database into a default choice for a generation of web startups.

s: Form ADV (Mar 2024) reports Saba Capital managing $13.4B of discretionary assets for 37 clients; Weinstein is managing member of the general partner
m: $13.4B x roughly 1.25% management fee = about $170M of annual fee revenue; a management company at 4x fee revenue is roughly $670M, majority-owned by him, plus his own capital in the funds
did: Ran Deutsche Bank's credit proprietary desk from 1998, spun it out as Saba Capital in 2009, and in 2012 took the other side of JPMorgan's London Whale credit index position, making roughly $300M as the bank lost $6.2B. He now runs about $13B and wages activist campaigns against closed-end funds.
why: Credit index arbitrage is mechanical: when one desk gets large enough to distort the price of an index against its own constituents, the basis is a hedged, self-correcting trade rather than a directional call. He looks for the same dislocation in closed-end funds trading below net asset value.
comp: BlackRock in the closed-end fund fights
obst: His Deutsche Bank desk lost roughly $1.8B in 2008 and was shut down; Saba then lost about 11% in 2012 and assets fell from $5.5B to under $2B before the volatility strategy came back in 2020.
turn: The 2012 London Whale trade, which made a spun-out prop trader into a name institutions would allocate to.

s: Form ADV (2024) reports Starboard Value managing about $8.3B of discretionary assets for 15 clients; roughly $9B reported as of Feb 2025
m: $8.3B at a 1.5% and 20% activist fee structure implies roughly $125M of annual fee revenue; a management company at about 4x that, majority-held by Smith as managing member, plus his personal fund investment
did: Ran the Value and Opportunity funds at Ramius, spun them out as Starboard Value in 2011, and in October 2014 replaced all twelve Darden Restaurants directors after a 294-slide deck on Olive Garden's unsalted pasta water and unlimited breadsticks; has since pressed Yahoo, Papa John's, Salesforce and Pfizer.
why: He does not need to own the company, he needs to convince the index funds. Vanguard, BlackRock and State Street own a quarter of every mid-cap and vote by governance policy, so a public research document detailed enough to justify their vote turns a 5% economic stake into working control of a board.
obst: Darden pre-emptively sold Red Lobster in 2014 without a shareholder vote specifically to blunt his campaign, forcing him into an unprecedented full-board replacement; later campaigns at Bristol-Myers Squibb and Papa John's stalled or ended in settlements.
turn: The October 2014 Darden vote, the first time a public company's entire board was swept out by an activist.

s: Forbes profile, $500M as of 4 Aug 2021 (Americas Richest Self-Made Women)
m: Last published Forbes figure, now five years old; carried forward unchanged
did: After seventeen years as a Vogue editor and two as a Ralph Lauren design director, opened a bridal salon in the Carlyle Hotel in 1990 at 40 because she could not find a wedding dress she liked; built it into a licensing house spanning Zales jewellery, Simply Vera at Kohl's, David's Bridal and fragrance.
why: Bridal was a large, fragmented category with no designer name at the top and a customer who buys once and does not price-shop. A $10,000 gown at the Carlyle anchored a pyramid that sold $70 dresses at David's Bridal under the same signature - the top of the pyramid was advertising, the bottom was the business.
obst: She was passed over for the editor-in-chief job at Vogue in 1987, which pushed her out of the only career she had; she then started a company at 40 with no manufacturing experience and no brand.
turn: Designing Nancy Kerrigan's costumes for the 1994 Winter Olympics, which put the name in front of a national television audience.

s: WallStreetZen insider ownership table for SHOO: 9,253,888 shares, 12.65% of the company, valued $438.08M
m: 9,253,888 shares x market price on 21 Aug 2026 = $438M; he is the largest individual holder
did: Started Steve Madden Ltd in Long Island City in 1990 with $1,100, selling chunky platform shoes out of the boot of his car to Manhattan boutiques; took it public in 1993, served 31 months in federal prison from 2005 for securities fraud tied to Stratton Oakmont, and returned as creative chief.
why: He compressed design-to-shelf to about six weeks by keeping sample-making in house and using near-shore production, so the company chased a trend that was already happening while Nine West and Nike were committed to forecasts made a year earlier. In fashion footwear, speed is the entire margin.
obst: He was convicted in 2001 of securities fraud and money laundering for his role in Stratton Oakmont's IPO manipulation, had to resign as chief executive, and ran the brand's design from a federal prison camp between 2005 and 2007.
turn: The 1993 IPO underwritten by Stratton Oakmont, which funded the first retail stores and a decade later nearly destroyed him.

s: Chainalysis last valued at about $8.6B after raising $538M across nine rounds; Levin is co-founder and, since Dec 2024, chief executive
m: A founding chief executive's residual stake after nine rounds is typically about 5% of equity; 5% x $8.6B = roughly $0.43B
did: Co-founded Chainalysis in New York in 2014 after running the bitcoin analytics project Coinometrics as an Oxford economics researcher; the company traces blockchain flows for the FBI, IRS, DEA and Europol as well as exchanges and banks, and he became chief executive in December 2024.
why: Bitcoin's ledger is permanent and public, so clustering heuristics can attach real names to pseudonymous addresses - and every subpoena, exchange integration and seizure adds labels to the graph. The dataset compounds and cannot be replicated by a later entrant with better software.
obst: The company was born out of the 2014 Mt. Gox collapse into a crypto community that saw transaction tracing as a betrayal of the technology's purpose, and had to sell surveillance software to governments while its customers were the exchanges being watched.
turn: Tracing the coins stolen from Mt. Gox, which won the first US federal law-enforcement contracts.

s: Forbes profile, $410M as of 3 Jun 2025 (Americas Richest Self-Made Women)
m: Published Forbes figure for a sub-billion self-made fortune
did: A lawyer at Cowen who moved into distressed debt, she founded Amroc Investments with her brother Marc Lasry in 1989 to trade bank loans and bankruptcy claims, then co-founded Avenue Capital in 1995, where she is president and managing partner running operations, legal and compliance across eleven offices.
why: Amroc made a market in trade claims - the unpaid invoices owed by bankrupt companies to their suppliers - which nobody else was pricing. That gave Avenue proprietary access to distressed paper before it ever reached the syndicated loan market, and the claims desk fed the fund its inventory.
obst: She built a distressed credit firm as a woman in early-1990s New York with no bank sponsorship and no institutional track record; Avenue's flagship then fell about 25% in 2008 and the firm had to gate redemptions and shrink.
turn: Selling Amroc and launching Avenue Capital in 1995 with $7M of the siblings own money.

s: Forbes (Nov 2018) reported Turner and Weinberg each netted about $250M from Roche's $1.9B purchase of Flatiron Health in Feb 2018
m: Reported $250M of deal proceeds plus his equity in Collectors, taken private at $850M in 2021, and the Operator Partners fund
did: Sold his first company, ad-targeting startup Invite Media, to Google for $81M in 2010 at 25; founded Flatiron Health in 2012 with Zach Weinberg after a cousin's leukaemia diagnosis and sold it to Roche for $1.9B in 2018; then led the $850M buyout of Collectors, owner of PSA grading.
why: About 96% of US cancer patients are treated outside academic trials, so their outcomes existed only as free text in clinic notes. Flatiron paid trained nurses to abstract those notes into structured records, then sold the evidence to drug makers who needed control arms the FDA would accept.
obst: Building the dataset meant buying and operating an actual electronic health record business - Altos Solutions in 2014 - and persuading hundreds of independent community oncology practices to hand over patient records under HIPAA before there was any product to show them.
turn: The February 2018 Roche acquisition, which paid $1.9B for a data asset rather than for software.

s: Take-Two 2026 proxy statement filed 15 Jul 2026: Zelnick beneficially owns 1,382,568 shares; TTWO closed $239.62 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 1,382,568 shares x $239.62 = $331.3M, including 1,126,165 restricted units held through ZMC Advisors
did: Ran 20th Century Fox's television arm and then BMG Entertainment, founded ZelnickMedia in 2001, and in 2007 his firm took control of Take-Two Interactive in a shareholder revolt after an options-backdating scandal; he has been chairman and chief executive ever since, through Grand Theft Auto V and NBA 2K.
why: ZMC's management agreement paid in Take-Two equity, so he was compensated like an owner of a company he never bought. He then protected Rockstar's schedule - letting Grand Theft Auto titles slip years rather than shipping annually - which kept each release an event instead of a product line.
obst: He inherited Take-Two mid-scandal with the SEC investigating backdated options and the founder indicted, then rejected a hostile $2B bid from Electronic Arts in 2008 with the stock falling; Grand Theft Auto VI slipped repeatedly and the shares fell hard in 2025.
turn: The March 2007 shareholder meeting that removed the incumbent board and installed ZelnickMedia as management.

s: Forbes (Nov 2018) reported Turner and Weinberg each netted about $250M from Roche's $1.9B purchase of Flatiron Health in Feb 2018
m: Reported $250M of deal proceeds, net of tax, plus his stakes in Operator Partners and Curie.Bio
did: Co-founded Invite Media with Nat Turner at Penn and sold it to Google for $81M in 2010, then co-founded Flatiron Health in 2012 as president, running product and engineering until Roche bought it for $1.9B in 2018; now runs Operator Partners, which invests only alongside operators, and co-founded Curie.Bio.
why: The pair split the company cleanly - Turner sold, Weinberg built - and the real moat was not software but the abstraction workforce: thousands of trained clinical staff converting free-text oncology notes into structured fields, an operating cost no software-only competitor was willing to carry.
obst: Google shut Invite Media's brand inside DoubleClick and the founders left early with the product buried; Flatiron then took $175M from Roche in 2016 while selling data to the same company, a conflict rival pharma customers and investors flagged loudly.
turn: The 2014 acquisition of Altos Solutions, which gave Flatiron the electronic health record that generated its data.

s: Sequential Brands acquired Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia for $353M in Dec 2015; Stewart held roughly 44% of the economics
m: Roughly 44% of the $353M sale plus earlier disclosed share sales, 1999 IPO proceeds and continuing licensing income from Marquee Brands
did: A former stockbroker who started a Westport catering business in 1976, published Entertaining in 1982, launched Martha Stewart Living in 1990, took the company public in 1999, served five months in federal prison in 2004 over an ImClone stock sale, and sold the company to Sequential Brands for $353M in 2015.
why: She was the first person to license one lifestyle name across a magazine, a television show and a mass retailer simultaneously. Buying her name and archive back from Time Warner in 1997 meant every Kmart towel and every advertising page paid the same owner - the brand, not the content, was the asset.
comp: Meredith and Better Homes and Gardens
obst: Her 2004 conviction for obstruction and false statements over the ImClone sale cost her five months in prison, sent the stock down about 80%, drove advertisers away and barred her from serving as a director of her own public company until 2011.
turn: The 1997 buyback of her name and archive from Time Warner, which created Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia.

s: Form 4, 14 Aug 2026: 2,105,480 CHEF shares held directly plus 24,793 in GRATs; CHEF closed $110.61 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 2,130,273 shares x $110.61 = $235.6M; excludes prior disclosed sales
did: With his brother John built Dairyland USA in the Bronx from a single truck delivering specialty cheese and produce to Manhattan chefs, renamed it The Chefs' Warehouse, took it public on Nasdaq in 2011 and rolled up dozens of regional specialty distributors.
why: Broadline distributors carry ten thousand commodity items at thin margins and compete on price. Chefs Warehouse carries fifty thousand specialty items - imported cheese, truffles, artisan oils - at nearly double the gross margin, because a chef who needs one specific French butter will pay for the truck.
obst: Covid closed white-tablecloth restaurants overnight in March 2020 and revenue fell by more than half in a quarter; the company drew down its revolver, suspended acquisitions and had to hold on to a perishable-inventory business with no customers.
turn: The July 2011 Nasdaq IPO, which funded a decade of regional distributor acquisitions.

s: Schedule 13G/A: 3,274,866 Vita Coco shares (5.6%) as of 27 Apr 2026, including 1,154,797 exercisable options; COCO closed $63.35 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 3,274,866 shares x $63.35 = $207.4M, before roughly $6M of disclosed 2026 sales
did: A software salesman who met two Brazilian women in a Manhattan bar in 2003 and learned about agua de coco; with Ira Liran founded Vita Coco in 2004 importing coconut water in Tetra Pak, sold minority stakes to Verlinvest and the Red Bull founding family, and listed on Nasdaq in October 2021.
why: He seeded the product through New York bodegas and yoga studios rather than supermarket shelves, so it looked like a discovery rather than a launch. Then he locked up aseptic coconut-processing capacity in the Philippines and Brazil, so when Coca-Cola and PepsiCo entered the category they could not get supply.
obst: Coca-Cola and PepsiCo each bought a rival coconut water brand from 2009 and outspent him roughly tenfold; a 2011 class action over sugar and electrolyte label claims forced independent retesting and a settlement that nearly broke a young company.
turn: Coca-Cola's retreat from Zico around 2014, after which Vita Coco took more than half the category.

s: Yahoo acquired Tumblr for $1.1B in cash, May 2013; Karp's stake was widely reported at about 25%
m: 25% x $1.1B = roughly $275M pre-tax, plus a reported $110M retention package vesting through 2017, net of tax
did: Left high school at 15, worked at Frederator Studios, and launched Tumblr in February 2007 at 20 as a short-form blogging platform; sold it to Yahoo for $1.1B in cash in May 2013 holding roughly a quarter of the company.
why: Reblogging collapsed the distinction between publishing and sharing - every post was simultaneously content and a distribution event - so a team of twenty carried a hundred million blogs with almost no marketing spend, and the fandom communities that formed there existed nowhere else.
obst: He had resisted advertising for years and sold a platform with almost no revenue; Yahoo wrote off $712M of the purchase price by 2016, the 2018 adult-content ban destroyed much of the community, and Verizon sold Tumblr to Automattic in 2019 for a reported $3M.
turn: The May 2013 Yahoo acquisition, agreed in cash before the advertising model was ever proven.

s: Form 4, 6 Jul 2026: 31,112 Class A shares direct, 4,555,404 Class B direct and 1,656,770 Class B held by the David A. Gilboa 2012 Family Trust; WRBY closed $27.44 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 6,243,286 combined shares x $27.44 = $171.3M
did: Co-founded Warby Parker in 2010 at Wharton with Neil Blumenthal, Jeff Raider and Andrew Hunt after losing a $700 pair of glasses on a flight; sells prescription eyewear direct at $95 with a five-frame home try-on box, and direct-listed on the NYSE in September 2021.
why: Prescription eyewear is a cheap medical device sold at a luxury markup because one company owned the frames, the brands, the retail chains and the vision insurance plan at once. Designing in house and selling direct captured that entire margin stack, and the try-on box solved the only thing e-commerce could not: fit.
obst: Four students with no optical industry contacts were refused by frame manufacturers unwilling to risk their Luxottica relationships; after the 2021 direct listing the shares fell more than 70% as physical store expansion consumed cash.
turn: Opening the first physical store in 2013 - the online company now takes most of its growth from roughly 300 shops.

s: Form 4, 1 May 2026: 137,262 Goldman Sachs shares held directly plus 16,171 in a family trust; GS closed $1,039.28 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 153,433 shares x $1,039.28 = $159.5M; excludes unvested restricted stock and prior disclosed sales
did: Joined Goldman Sachs in 1999 as a rare direct-entry partner from Bear Stearns, built its high-yield and leveraged finance business, ran the investment banking division from 2006 and has been chief executive since October 2018.
why: The Goldman partnership pays in restricted stock that cannot be sold for years, so two decades inside the firm's highest-margin business compounds into an eight-figure annual equity grant. The wealth is a function of tenure at the fee pool, not of a founding stake.
obst: The 1MDB scandal broke months into his tenure - Goldman paid $2.9B in 2020 and clawed back $174M from executives including $10M of his own pay - and the Marcus consumer bank lost over $6B before he shut it down in 2023 amid open partner dissent.
turn: The October 2018 succession contest against Harvey Schwartz, which he won and which vested the largest equity grants of his career.

s: WallStreetZen insider ownership table: 29,411,895 Shutterstock shares; SSTK closed $5.32 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 29,411,895 shares x $5.32 = $156.5M; the stake was worth over $850M a year earlier before the stock fell from $29.50
did: A programmer who bought a camera, shot 30,000 of his own images and launched Shutterstock in 2003 as a $49-a-month unlimited-download subscription; bootstrapped it for four years, took Insight money in 2007, listed on the NYSE in 2012 and stepped down as chief executive in 2020. He now runs Pareto Holdings.
why: Stock photography sold single images for hundreds of dollars through agency reps who negotiated usage rights. A flat monthly subscription, served over a contributor network paid per download, inverted both the cost structure and the buying decision - and the marginal cost of one more download was zero.
obst: He bootstrapped for four years against a Getty near-monopoly with no capital; then from 2023 generative image models collapsed demand for licensed stock, Shutterstock fell from about $29.50 to $5.32 in the year to August 2026 and the Getty merger failed.
turn: The October 2012 NYSE IPO, in which he retained a majority stake and became New York's first bootstrapped internet billionaire on paper.

s: Form 4, May 2026: 4,890,781 Braze Class A shares held directly plus 470 indirect; BRZE closed $31.06 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 4,891,251 shares x $31.06 = $151.9M, including 669,747 unvested restricted and performance units
did: Co-founded Appboy at a Manhattan hackathon in 2011 with Jon Hyman and Mark Ghermezian, building a customer-engagement platform for targeted mobile push and in-app messaging; renamed it Braze in 2017 and listed on Nasdaq in November 2021.
why: Marketing clouds were built around email and the web and reached the customer after the fact. Braze started from the mobile SDK inside the app, so it held the live behavioural event stream - what the user did thirty seconds ago - which Salesforce and Adobe could only import later from a warehouse.
obst: Two MIT engineers with no enterprise sales experience spent the first two years selling to app startups with no budget and high mortality; after the 2021 IPO the shares fell more than 70% as software multiples compressed.
turn: The 2015 Series B and the deliberate move upmarket from app developers to enterprise brands.

s: Estee Lauder acquired Bobbi Brown Essentials in 1995 for a reported $74.5M; Jones Road Beauty, founded 2020, reached roughly $150M of annual sales
m: 1995 sale proceeds plus 22 years of Estee Lauder executive pay, plus a majority family stake in Jones Road marked at roughly 3x revenue
co: Bobbi Brown Cosmetics and Jones Road Beauty
did: A freelance makeup artist who created ten brown-based lipsticks with a chemist in 1991 and sold them at Bergdorf Goodman; Estee Lauder bought the company in 1995, she stayed 22 years, left in 2016, and once the non-compete expired launched Jones Road Beauty in 2020.
why: Prestige counters in 1991 sold theatrical seasonal colour. She sold the opposite proposition - that makeup should look like skin - as a ten-item system rather than a collection, which meant a customer bought the whole range once instead of one lipstick a season.
obst: Selling to Estee Lauder in 1995 meant she did not own her own name; when she walked away in 2016 she could not use it, could not reference her own back catalogue and had to build a second brand from nothing at 63.
turn: The 2020 launch of Jones Road, seeded on TikTok around a $60 multipurpose balm and grown to nine figures with no department store.

s: Forbes profile, real-time net worth $3.4B as of 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes figure: Forbes reports he owns 32% of Bilt Rewards, which raised $250M at a $10.75B valuation in July 2025
did: Founded Bilt Rewards in 2021, a loyalty network that lets renters earn points on rent with no transaction fee charged to the landlord, funded instead by a Wells Fargo co-branded card; it raised $250M at a $10.75B valuation in July 2025 and he owns 32% of it.
why: Rent is the largest recurring consumer payment in America and the card networks could never reach it, because landlords refuse to absorb a 3% interchange fee. Bilt routes the payment so the landlord pays nothing and the issuer funds the points, opening a trillion dollars of uncardable spend.
obst: Wells Fargo was reported in 2024 to be losing roughly $10M a month on the co-brand because customers paid rent, took the points and never revolved a balance, and the bank publicly weighed walking away - forcing Jain to re-cut the economics and bring in a second issuer.
turn: The 2021 Wells Fargo co-brand agreement, which turned a rent-points idea into a funded payments network.

s: Forbes profile, real-time net worth $1.9B as of 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes figure: Forbes reports each of the three Ramp cofounders owns about 6% of a company private investors valued at $32B in Nov 2025
did: Co-founded Ramp in 2019 with Karim Atiyeh and Gene Lee after selling their price-tracking app Paribus to Capital One in 2016; Ramp issues corporate cards with expense software designed to cut customer spending, and investors valued it at $32B in November 2025 and $44B in June 2026.
why: Every corporate card issuer earns interchange on spend, so all of them were paid to encourage more of it. Ramp inverted the pitch - software that cancels duplicate subscriptions and forces vendor renegotiation - and won finance departments by promising to shrink the very number it earns a fee on.
obst: They launched a corporate card in 2019 into a market where Brex had already raised hundreds of millions and locked up venture-backed startups, then hit the March 2020 shutdown when business spending collapsed and card volume - their only revenue line - disappeared.
turn: The 2022 launch of bill pay and procurement, which moved Ramp from a card to the whole finance stack and took the valuation from $8B to $32B.

s: Forbes profile, real-time net worth $1.9B as of 21 Aug 2026

did: Joined Paribus as a software engineer in 2015, followed the founders to Capital One after the 2016 acquisition, and in 2019 co-founded Ramp with Eric Glyman and Karim Atiyeh, building the engineering organisation behind its corporate card and spend-management platform.
why: Ramp built the ledger, the card issuing and the accounting integrations as one system instead of bolting software onto a bank partner's rails, so it can act on a transaction as it happens - declining a duplicate software renewal at the point of sale, which a downstream expense tool can only flag a month later.
obst: Three people with a consumer price-tracking app on their record had to obtain bank partnerships and card-issuing capability from scratch and sell to corporate finance departments, against a rival that had already raised far more and owned the segment.
turn: The 2020 decision to compete on spend controls rather than card rewards, taken during the pandemic collapse in business spending.

s: Forbes profile: Glossier has raised $266M and was last valued at $1.8B
m: A founder-CEO who raised $266M across six rounds typically retains roughly 15% of equity; 15% x $1.8B = about $0.27B
did: Turned her beauty blog Into The Gloss, started in 2010 while a Vogue assistant, into Glossier in 2014, launching with four products sold direct to readers who had been commenting on the blog for four years; she stepped down as chief executive in June 2022 and remains the largest individual holder.
why: She built the audience before the product. Into The Gloss ran interviews asking women what was actually on their bathroom shelves, so Glossier launched with four years of documented demand and a customer list, and the products were specified from comment threads rather than a lab brief.
obst: Glossier laid off more than a third of its staff in January 2022 after over-hiring into a technology strategy that never shipped and shutting the Glossier Play spinoff; she resigned as chief executive five months later and the brand had to abandon its direct-only doctrine and sell through Sephora.
turn: The 2016 launch of Boy Brow, a single $16 eyebrow product that sold out repeatedly and became the entry point for millions of customers.
